# Can Law Enforcement Store CSAM Evidence in the Cloud?


November 23, 2026


|[Ryan Parthemore - Law Enforcement Veteran, Cellebrite Digital Intelligence and Forensics Solutions](https://cellebrite.com/en/author/ryanparthemore/)


Law enforcement agencies can store child sexual abuse material (CSAM) evidence in the cloud, as long as the repository does more than hold files: it has to require two-factor authentication, encrypt data in transit and at rest, and log every login and share. That access log gives agencies a chain-of-custody record that copies on USB drives never produce.


If offenders put CSAM in the cloud to run their operations, law enforcement has to use the same means to fight it, especially at today’s volume. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received[21.3 million CyberTipline reports in 2025](https://www.missingkids.org/gethelpnow/cybertipline/cybertiplinedata) , covering 61.8 million images, videos and other files. The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF)[confirmed 311,610 reports as CSAM](https://www.iwf.org.uk/annual-data-insights-report-2025) the same year, up 7% from 2024.


Each file is both evidence and contraband, and each one is a permanent record of a child’s abuse, so how an agency handles the file matters as much as what it proves. Sound CSAM evidence management starts with knowing why copies multiply, how a cloud repository reins them in, which security standards apply and what to ask a vendor before any evidence moves.


Cloud computing – Source: Shutterstock


## Every Handoff Creates Another Copy of CSAM Evidence


Teams copy CSAM evidence to physical media so they can collaborate. By the time a case reaches trial, one set of files can exist on five drives, and agency staff must track, secure and eventually destroy each one.


Follow one case. The examiner who identifies and catalogs the material knows it will be used in a criminal prosecution and, more importantly, to save a child. That examiner hands a copy to the investigator, and because agency policy treats that copy as original evidence, the investigator makes a working copy, which is not a bad idea when the drive may not outlast the case. When the victim’s age is in question, a forensic pediatrician needs a copy of their own. Prosecutors need one to build the case, and the submission to NCMEC’s Child Victim Identification Program (CVIP) takes another. Each copy exists for a good reason, and each one is a drive someone now has to account for.


Five copies later, agencies need answers to six questions:


- Who manages each copy?
- How does the agency secure each copy?
- How long does the media last?
- Who opened which copy, and when?
- Who destroys each copy, and does that meet policy?
- What does the agency tell a victim when a copy slips out of its control, or the evidence is missing at trial?


Copies on drives leave most of them unanswered. A central repository can answer all six from one place.

## How Does a Cloud Repository Control CSAM Evidence?


A cloud repository replaces scattered copies with one controlled source. Authorized users reach the evidence over a network connection, and the system records every login, share and access. Agencies grant, review and revoke access in one place instead of tracking drives in drawers. Fewer copies also means fewer places a child’s images can be lost, stolen or seen by someone with no need to see them.


Connectivity is the root problem. People in various roles at multiple agencies and organizations must work together for justice to be served, and when they can’t reach the same system, the evidence travels on drives. Give them one secure place to reach the same files and most of those copies never get made. The same pattern shows up with digital evidence of every kind, along with the same[objections to moving it to the cloud](https://cellebrite.com/en/blog/rethinking-digital-evidence-sharing-moving-beyond-old-habits-for-modern-policing/) .


Compliance frameworks capture the requirements a cloud repository has to meet before it can stand in for the evidence room. Look for Zero Trust architecture as NIST defines it in SP 800-207, plus two-factor authentication and encryption in transit and at rest. A USB drive in a drawer is only as secure as the drawer, and it records nothing about who plugged it in.


## Which Security Standards Apply to Cloud CSAM Evidence?


The standard depends on the agency’s country and type. In the U.S.,[Guardian meets CJIS Security Policy requirements](https://cellebrite.com/en/products/guardian/) for agencies subject to CJIS. For U.S. federal agencies, Guardian Collaborate is available in a FedRAMP High Authorized environment through the Cellebrite Government Cloud. In Australia, Guardian has been independently assessed under the Infosec Registered Assessors Program (IRAP) at the PROTECTED tier. For agencies with data residency obligations, Guardian Investigate offers EU regional deployment.


Each one covers a specific product and region, so confirm which applies to the Guardian package an agency buys before any CSAM evidence moves.


## What Should Agencies Ask Before Moving CSAM Evidence to the Cloud?


Start with the agency’s own retention and destruction policy, since state law and agency priorities set those rules. Then ask where the data lives, who at the vendor can reach it, which standards cover the specific product, how the system logs access, and how it enforces retention and destruction. Written answers to those five questions show whether a repository fits agency policy.


A central repository also concentrates risk in one place, which raises the stakes on every answer.


## How Does Cellebrite Guardian Control Access to CSAM Evidence?


Cellebrite Guardian is cloud-native digital evidence management software that connects investigators, examiners, prosecutors and others in one workspace, so case teams share evidence across the whole investigation without passing drives between agencies.


The copies start in the lab, so that is where Guardian picks up the evidence. It integrates natively with Cellebrite Inseyets (UFED and Physical Analyzer), so extractions transfer automatically from the lab to the cloud, preserving chain of custody from the moment of seizure through prosecution with no manual file transfers. The first handoff in the five-copy chain never touches a drive.


For CSAM cases, the first control is who can see the files at all: role-based permissions let only authorized personnel view, download or modify evidence. Each upload can also be tagged as Suspected CSAM, which flags the file’s sensitive status and triggers special handling to prevent unintentional sharing.


Guardian records system events such as logins, uploads, downloads and file views in tamper-evident audit trails, and the Activity Report and Chain of Custody Report show who had access to evidence and whether they viewed it. It also meets the baseline from earlier: encryption at rest and in transit, Zero Trust architecture and two-factor authentication. The case team gets one source of truth for the evidence and a record of everyone who touched it.

## Common Questions About Cloud CSAM Evidence


### Can agencies store CSAM evidence in the cloud?


Yes, when the repository enforces two-factor authentication, encrypts data in transit and at rest, and logs access. State law and agency policy still govern retention and destruction.


### Who decides when CSAM evidence is destroyed?


State legislation and agency priorities set the rules. Each agency defines its policy and checks that its repository can enforce it.


### How does cloud storage reduce the risk of revictimization?


Every copy of CSAM evidence is another place a child’s images can be lost, stolen or seen without need. One controlled repository cuts the number of copies and logs who viewed each file.
